questions.q: Which animal says moo?
questions.explain: A cow says moo. A cat says meow and a duck says quack.
questions.tip: Moo, moo! The cow says moo.

questions.q: Which animal has feathers?
questions.explain: Birds have feathers. Dogs have fur and fish have scales.
questions.tip: Birds wear a coat of feathers.

questions.q: Which animal lives in water and has fins?
questions.explain: A fish lives in water and swims with its fins.
questions.tip: Fish swim, swish, swish, with their fins.

questions.q: What covers a dog's body?
questions.explain: A dog is covered in soft fur. Birds have feathers and fish have scales.
questions.tip: Pet a dog and feel its furry fur.

questions.q: Which animal is very big and has a long trunk?
questions.explain: An elephant is the biggest animal on land. It uses its long trunk to drink and to pick things up.
questions.tip: An elephant's trunk is a nose that can hold things!

questions.q: What do birds build to keep their eggs safe?
questions.explain: Birds build nests from twigs and grass, then lay their eggs inside.
questions.tip: A nest is a little bed for bird eggs.

questions.q: Which animal hops?
questions.explain: Rabbits hop on their strong back legs. Snakes slide and fish swim.
questions.tip: Hop, hop, hop, like a bunny!

questions.q: What do baby kittens and puppies drink from their moms?
questions.explain: Baby kittens and puppies drink their mother's milk, just like human babies do.
questions.tip: Baby animals say: milk, please!

questions.q: What do you use to see?
questions.explain: Your eyes let you see colors, shapes and your friends.
questions.tip: Blink, blink! Your eyes see the world.

questions.q: How many hands do you have?
questions.explain: You have two hands, and each hand has five fingers.
questions.tip: Clap! It takes two hands to clap.

questions.q: What do you use to walk and run?
questions.explain: Your legs and feet carry you when you walk, run and jump.
questions.tip: Legs go walk, walk, run, run!

questions.q: What do you chew food with?
questions.explain: Your teeth chew food into small bits so you can swallow it.
questions.tip: Crunch, crunch! Teeth chew your lunch.

questions.q: Which part is at the top of your body?
questions.explain: Your head is at the top. Your feet are at the bottom.
questions.tip: Head, shoulders, knees and toes: head is first!

questions.q: What do you use to grab a toy?
questions.explain: Your hands and fingers can grab, hold and squeeze.
questions.tip: Grab it with your hands!

questions.q: What should you do before you eat?
questions.explain: Washing your hands with soap gets rid of germs that could make you sick.
questions.tip: Soap and water, scrub, scrub, scrub, before you eat.

questions.q: What does your body need to grow big and strong?
questions.explain: Healthy food, water, play and plenty of sleep help your body grow.
questions.tip: Eat, play, sleep, grow!

questions.q: What falls from the clouds when it rains?
questions.explain: Rain is drops of water falling from clouds.
questions.tip: Pitter-patter, raindrops are water.

questions.q: What keeps you dry in the rain?
questions.explain: An umbrella or a raincoat keeps the rain off you.
questions.tip: Pop open an umbrella and stay dry!

questions.q: What warms you up on a sunny day?
questions.explain: The sun gives us light and warmth.
questions.tip: The sun is like a big warm lamp in the sky.

questions.q: Snow is...
questions.explain: Snow is frozen water, so it is very cold.
questions.tip: Brr! Snow is cold, so wear your mittens.

questions.q: What makes a kite fly?
questions.explain: Wind is moving air. It pushes the kite up into the sky.
questions.tip: Whoosh! Wind lifts the kite.

questions.q: What is a rainbow?
choices: Colors in the sky after rain
questions.explain: When the sun shines through raindrops, you can see a rainbow of colors in the sky.
questions.tip: Sun plus rain can make a rainbow.

questions.q: What do you wear when it is cold outside?
questions.explain: A warm coat, hat and mittens keep you warm in cold weather.
questions.tip: Cold outside? Coat on!

questions.q: What is the loud boom you hear in a storm?
questions.explain: Thunder is the loud sound that comes with lightning in a storm.
questions.tip: Flash of lightning, then boom goes the thunder.

questions.q: What do you use to smell a flower?
questions.explain: Your nose smells things, like flowers and cookies baking.
questions.tip: Sniff, sniff! Your nose knows.

questions.q: What do you use to hear music?
questions.explain: Your ears hear sounds, like music, voices and birds.
questions.tip: You hear with your ears.

questions.q: What do you use to taste ice cream?
questions.explain: Your tongue tastes food: sweet, sour, salty and more.
questions.tip: Lick an ice cream cone: your tongue tastes it!

questions.q: Which one is soft to touch?
questions.explain: A kitten's fur is soft. Rocks and bricks are hard.
questions.tip: Soft kitty, warm kitty, fluffy fur.

questions.q: Which one is loud?
questions.explain: A drum makes a loud sound when you hit it. A feather and a pillow are quiet.
questions.tip: Boom, boom! A drum is loud.

questions.q: Which one tastes sweet?
questions.explain: Cookies taste sweet. Lemons taste sour and salt tastes salty.
questions.tip: Sweet treat: a cookie!

questions.q: Which one feels hot?
questions.explain: Soup from the stove is hot. Ice and snow are cold.
questions.tip: Hot soup: blow on it first!

questions.q: How many senses do you have?
questions.explain: You have five senses: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.
questions.tip: Five senses, five fingers: count them on one hand!

questions.q: When do we see the sun?
questions.explain: The sun shines in the daytime. At night our side of Earth faces away from it.
questions.tip: Sun up, it's day. Sun down, it's night.

questions.q: What twinkles in the sky at night?
questions.explain: Stars are far-away suns. We see them twinkle when the sky is dark.
questions.tip: Twinkle, twinkle, little star.

questions.q: When do most people sleep?
questions.explain: Most people sleep at night when it is dark and wake up in the morning.
questions.tip: Dark sky, sleepy eyes: it's bedtime.

questions.q: The sun comes up in the...
questions.say: The sun comes up in the what?
questions.explain: The sun rises in the morning and goes down in the evening.
questions.tip: Good morning, sun!

questions.q: When it is dark outside, it is...
questions.say: When it is dark outside, it is what?
questions.explain: Night is the dark part of the day, when the sun is not shining on us.
questions.tip: Dark means night; bright means day.

questions.q: What lights up the daytime sky?
questions.explain: The sun lights up the sky and the ground all day long.
questions.tip: Daytime is sun time.

questions.q: Which animal is awake at night and says hoo?
questions.explain: Owls hunt at night and sleep in the day. Chickens and butterflies are awake in the daytime.
questions.tip: Hoo, hoo! The owl is up all night.

questions.q: What do you do when you wake up in the morning?
questions.explain: In the morning you wake up, get out of bed and start your day.
questions.tip: Morning: up and out of bed!

questions.q: Which animal is a mammal?
questions.explain: Mammals breathe air and feed their babies milk. Dolphins do both, even though they live in the sea.
questions.tip: Mammals make milk: dolphins, dogs, and you!

questions.q: What is a baby frog called?
questions.explain: A tadpole lives in water and grows legs as it turns into a frog.
questions.tip: A tadpole has a tail like a tiny fish, then it grows legs.

questions.q: A butterfly starts its life as an egg. What does the egg hatch into?
questions.explain: Egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly: that is the butterfly's life cycle.
questions.tip: The very hungry caterpillar eats and eats, then becomes a butterfly.

questions.q: Which animal lives in the ocean?
questions.explain: An octopus lives in salty ocean water and has eight arms.
questions.tip: Octo means eight: an octopus has eight arms.

questions.q: What do honeybees make?
questions.explain: Honeybees turn the nectar from flowers into honey.
questions.tip: Busy honeybees make sweet honey.

questions.q: What do we call an animal that eats only plants?
questions.explain: Herbivores eat plants, like cows and rabbits. Carnivores eat meat.
questions.tip: Herbivores eat herbs and greens; carnivores chomp meat.

questions.q: How many legs does an insect have?
questions.explain: Insects have 6 legs. Spiders have 8, so spiders are not insects.
questions.tip: Insects have six legs: ants, bees and beetles all walk on six.

questions.q: Which animal hatches from an egg?
questions.explain: Birds hatch from eggs. Most reptiles and fish lay eggs too. Cows, dogs and horses are born live.
questions.tip: Which came first? For a chick, the egg!

questions.q: Polar bears live in a habitat that is very cold and icy. What is it called?
questions.explain: Polar bears live in the Arctic, the icy land and sea near the North Pole. Penguins live far away, near the South Pole.
questions.tip: Polar bears live near the North Pole, in the Arctic.

questions.q: What do plants use to make their own food?
questions.explain: Plants use sunlight, water and air to make their own food in their leaves.
questions.tip: Plants eat sunshine: sun plus water plus air makes plant food.

questions.q: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
questions.explain: Roots grow down into the soil and drink up water.
questions.tip: Roots are like straws under the ground.

questions.q: Which part of a plant makes most of its food?
questions.explain: Green leaves catch sunlight and make food for the plant.
questions.tip: Leaves are the plant's kitchen.

questions.q: Which one is a fruit?
questions.explain: A fruit grows from a flower and holds seeds. An apple has seeds inside.
questions.tip: Cut an apple open: seeds inside means it is a fruit.

questions.q: Which one is NOT a living thing?
questions.say: Which one is not a living thing?
questions.explain: Living things grow, need food and water, and make new living things. A rock does none of these.
questions.tip: A rock never eats, drinks or grows.

questions.q: What does a seed grow into?
questions.explain: A seed has a tiny baby plant inside it. With water and warmth, it grows into a new plant.
questions.tip: Plant a seed, and a plant grows from it.

questions.q: What do bees carry from flower to flower that helps plants make seeds?
questions.explain: Pollen is a fine powder, often yellow. When bees carry it to another flower, the plant can make seeds.
questions.tip: Bees are pollen taxis for flowers.

questions.q: What does a green plant need to grow well?
questions.explain: Plants need water, sunlight and air to grow well.
questions.tip: Give a plant a drink and a sunny window.

questions.q: Which season comes after winter?
questions.explain: The seasons go winter, spring, summer, fall, and then winter again.
questions.tip: Spring springs up after winter.

questions.q: Which season is usually the coldest?
questions.explain: Winter is the coldest season in most places, with short days.
questions.tip: Winter means snowmen and mittens.

questions.q: Where does rain come from?
questions.explain: Tiny water drops in clouds join together, get heavy and fall as rain.
questions.tip: Clouds are like sponges in the sky: too full, and drip, drop!

questions.q: A desert gets very little...
questions.say: A desert gets very little what?
questions.explain: Deserts are dry places that get very little rain.
questions.tip: Desert has one s, like the one sip of rain it gets!

questions.q: Which tool measures how hot or cold it is?
questions.explain: A thermometer measures temperature.
questions.tip: Thermo means heat: a thermometer meters the heat.

questions.q: What makes a shadow?
questions.explain: A shadow forms where something blocks the light.
questions.tip: Stand in the sun: your body blocks the light, and your shadow appears.

questions.q: Water turns into ice when it gets...
questions.say: Water turns into ice when it gets what?
questions.explain: Water freezes into ice when it gets cold enough: 32 degrees Fahrenheit, or 0 degrees Celsius.
questions.tip: Put water in the freezer and it gets cold enough to turn to ice.

questions.q: What is frozen water that falls from clouds as soft white flakes?
questions.explain: Snowflakes are made of tiny bits of ice that fall from cold clouds.
questions.tip: No two snowflakes look exactly alike.

questions.q: Which one is a solid?
questions.explain: A solid keeps its own shape. Milk and juice are liquids, and steam is a gas.
questions.tip: Solids stay put: a rock keeps its shape.

questions.q: Which one is a liquid?
questions.explain: A liquid flows and takes the shape of its cup. Milk is a liquid.
questions.tip: Liquids pour: milk, juice and water.

questions.q: Which one is a gas?
questions.explain: A gas spreads out to fill its space. The air around us is a gas.
questions.tip: You can't see air, but you can feel it when the wind blows.

questions.q: Melting ice turns into...
questions.explain: When solid ice warms up, it melts into liquid water.
questions.tip: An ice cube in the sun becomes a puddle.

questions.q: When water boils, it turns into...
questions.say: When water boils, it turns into what?
questions.explain: Boiling water turns into steam, a gas called water vapor.
questions.tip: Watch a pot boil: the steam floats up.

questions.q: What happens to an ice cube in a warm room?
questions.explain: Warm air heats the ice, so it melts into water.
questions.tip: Warm makes ice melt; cold makes water freeze.

questions.q: Which rock can float on water?
questions.explain: Pumice comes from volcanoes and is full of tiny air bubbles, so it can float.
questions.tip: Pumice is a rock full of bubbles, like a sponge made of stone.

questions.q: Which one keeps its own shape?
questions.explain: A block of wood is a solid, so it keeps its shape. Liquids and gases take the shape of what they are in.
questions.tip: Pour juice into a bowl and it changes shape; a block stays a block.

questions.q: What is the closest star to Earth?
questions.explain: The Sun is a star, and it is the closest star to Earth. The Moon and the planets are not stars.
questions.tip: Our Sun is a star, the one we see every day.

questions.q: Which planet do we live on?
questions.explain: We live on Earth, the third planet from the Sun.
questions.tip: Mercury, Venus, Earth: we are number three.

questions.q: What pulls things down to the ground?
questions.explain: Gravity pulls things toward Earth. That is why a ball falls when you drop it.
questions.tip: What goes up must come down: thank gravity!

questions.q: Which one gives off its own light?
questions.explain: The Sun makes its own light. The Moon shines only because sunlight bounces off it.
questions.tip: The Moon is like a mirror for the Sun.

questions.q: Why is it night time?
choices: Our side of Earth turns away from the Sun
questions.explain: Earth spins all the time. When our side turns away from the Sun, it is night.
questions.tip: Earth spins like a top: day on the sunny side, night on the other.

questions.q: What are the hard parts inside your body that hold you up?
questions.explain: Your bones make up your skeleton. A grown-up has about 206 bones.
questions.tip: Without bones you would be as floppy as a noodle!

questions.q: Which sense do you use with your ears?
questions.explain: Ears hear, eyes see, the tongue tastes and the nose smells.
questions.tip: You hEAR with your EARs.

questions.q: Which part of your body pumps blood?
questions.explain: Your heart is a strong muscle that pumps blood all around your body.
questions.tip: Put your hand on your chest and feel your heart: thump, thump!

questions.q: Which part of your body helps you breathe?
questions.explain: Your lungs fill with air when you breathe in.
questions.tip: Take a deep breath: your lungs fill up like balloons.

questions.q: What does a caterpillar turn into?
questions.explain: A caterpillar is the larva of a butterfly (or a moth). It wraps itself in a chrysalis and comes out as a butterfly.
questions.tip: Egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly: the caterpillar is the hungry middle stage.

questions.q: Which stage comes between caterpillar and butterfly?
questions.explain: Inside the chrysalis, also called the pupa, the caterpillar's body changes into a butterfly.
questions.tip: The chrysalis is the butterfly's changing room.

questions.q: A tadpole grows legs and loses its tail as it becomes a...
questions.explain: Frogs start as eggs, hatch into tadpoles that breathe with gills, then grow legs and lungs.
questions.tip: Tadpole: tail first, then legs, then it's a frog.

questions.q: What is the first stage of a flowering plant's life cycle?
questions.explain: A plant starts as a seed, sprouts, grows leaves, makes flowers, and the flowers make fruit with new seeds.
questions.tip: Seed, sprout, plant, flower, fruit, and back to seed.

questions.q: Which animals go through metamorphosis, a big change in body shape as they grow?
questions.explain: Metamorphosis means a big change in form. A tadpole becomes a frog and a caterpillar becomes a butterfly. Puppies and calves just grow bigger.
questions.tip: Meta-MORPH-osis: the body morphs into a new shape.

questions.q: A baby chicken is a chick. What is a baby kangaroo called?
questions.explain: A baby kangaroo is a joey. It grows inside its mother's pouch. A cub is a baby bear, a kid is a baby goat and a calf is a baby cow.
questions.tip: Little Joey rides in Mom's pouch.

questions.q: What is pollination?
choices: Moving pollen from flower to flower so seeds can form
Cutting dead leaves off a plant
questions.explain: When pollen reaches another flower of the same kind, carried by bees, butterflies, birds or wind, the flower can make seeds.
questions.tip: Pollination = pollen on the move.

questions.q: Which of these spread seeds to new places?
questions.explain: Dandelion seeds ride the wind, coconuts float on water, and animals carry seeds in their fur or droppings.
questions.tip: Seeds travel by air, by water and by animal taxi.

questions.q: Complete metamorphosis has four stages: egg, larva, pupa and...
questions.explain: Butterflies, beetles and flies have four stages. The adult is the last one and lays new eggs.
questions.tip: ELPA: Egg, Larva, Pupa, Adult.

questions.q: What do we call it when an animal rests through the winter with a slow heartbeat?
questions.explain: Bats, ground squirrels and hedgehogs hibernate. Their bodies slow down to save energy when food is scarce. Bears do something similar, called winter torpor.
questions.tip: Hibernation is a long winter nap.

questions.q: Which animal lives in a hot, dry desert?
questions.explain: Camels can go a long time without water and have wide feet for walking on sand.
questions.tip: A camel's hump stores fat for long desert trips.

questions.q: Which habitat is hot and rainy, with more kinds of plants and animals than any other?
questions.explain: Tropical rainforests near the equator are warm and wet all year and are home to millions of species.
questions.tip: Rain plus forest equals rainforest: wet, warm and full of life.

questions.q: What is an animal that hunts and eats other animals called?
questions.explain: A predator hunts. The animal it catches is its prey.
questions.tip: PREDator preys; the PREY gets eaten.

questions.q: In a food chain, what do the arrows show?
choices: The direction energy moves, from what is eaten to what eats it
questions.explain: Grass -> rabbit -> fox: each arrow points from the food to the eater, showing where the energy goes.
questions.tip: The arrow means 'is eaten by'.

questions.q: Which is a producer in a food chain?
questions.explain: Producers are plants: they make their own food from sunlight. Animals are consumers because they eat other living things.
questions.tip: Producers produce their own food. That's plants.

questions.q: What is camouflage?
choices: Colors or patterns that help an animal hide
A loud call to find a mate
questions.explain: A stick insect looks like a twig and a snowshoe hare turns white in winter. Camouflage hides animals from predators or prey.
questions.tip: Camouflage: now you see me, now you don't.

questions.q: What do we call animals that eat both plants and meat?
questions.explain: Bears, raccoons and most people are omnivores. Herbivores eat only plants and carnivores eat only meat.
questions.tip: OMNI means all: omnivores eat all kinds of food.

questions.q: Which living things break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil?
questions.explain: Fungi, bacteria and worms are decomposers. Without them, dead leaves and animals would pile up forever.
questions.tip: Decomposers are nature's clean-up crew.

questions.q: Why do some birds fly south in the fall?
choices: To find food and warmer weather
To lay eggs in the snow
questions.explain: This is migration. Geese and many other birds fly to warmer places where they can find food, then come back in spring.
questions.tip: Migration: moving with the seasons.

questions.q: Which habitat is frozen most of the year, with no trees?
questions.explain: The tundra is the cold, treeless land near the Arctic. The ground stays frozen under the surface, so trees cannot grow.
questions.tip: Tundra: too cold for trees.

questions.q: What ocean habitat is built by tiny animals and is home to lots of colorful fish?
questions.explain: Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called coral polyps in warm, shallow seas.
questions.tip: A coral reef is an underwater city built by tiny animals.

questions.q: A ramp used to roll a wagon up to a porch is which simple machine?
questions.explain: An inclined plane is a slope. It lets you move something up with less force over a longer distance.
questions.tip: Inclined plane: a plain old ramp.

questions.q: A seesaw is an example of which simple machine?
questions.explain: A lever is a bar that turns on a point called the fulcrum. A seesaw's fulcrum is in the middle.
questions.tip: A lever lifts: seesaws, crowbars and bottle openers.

questions.q: Which simple machine uses a rope over a wheel to lift a flag up a pole?
questions.explain: A pulley changes the direction of your pull: you pull down and the flag goes up.
questions.tip: Pull-ey: pull down to lift up.

questions.q: An axe blade that splits wood is which simple machine?
questions.explain: A wedge is thick at one end and thin at the other. It pushes things apart. Knives and nails are wedges too.
questions.tip: A wedge wedges things apart.

questions.q: A doorknob is which simple machine?
questions.explain: The knob is a wheel and the rod inside is the axle. Turning the big knob makes it easier to turn the small axle.
questions.tip: Wheel and axle: a wheel on a stick, like a doorknob or a steering wheel.

questions.q: A screw is like which simple machine wrapped around a post?
questions.explain: The thread of a screw is a tiny ramp spiraling around a rod.
questions.tip: A screw is a ramp that went for a twist.

questions.q: What is a push or a pull called?
questions.explain: Forces are pushes and pulls. They can start, stop, speed up, slow down or turn things.
questions.tip: Force = push or pull.

questions.q: What force slows a ball rolling across a carpet?
questions.explain: Friction is the force between two surfaces that rub together. Rough carpet makes more friction than a smooth floor.
questions.tip: Friction is the rub that slows things down.

questions.q: Which force pulls a dropped ball down to the ground?
questions.explain: Gravity pulls everything toward the center of Earth.
questions.tip: Gravity: what goes up must come down.

questions.q: What do simple machines do?
choices: Make work easier by changing the force needed or its direction
questions.explain: A machine cannot give you free energy, but it can let you use a smaller force over a longer distance, or push instead of pull.
questions.tip: Simple machines: less force, more distance.

questions.q: What are the three common states of matter?
questions.explain: Ice is a solid, water is a liquid and steam is a gas. The same stuff can be in any of the three states.
questions.tip: Ice, water, steam: solid, liquid, gas.

questions.q: What is matter?
choices: Anything that takes up space and has mass
questions.explain: Air is matter even though you cannot see it: it takes up space and has mass.
questions.tip: If it takes up space, it's matter. Even air!

questions.q: What happens when a liquid freezes?
questions.explain: Freezing turns a liquid into a solid, like water into ice.
questions.tip: Freeze: liquid to solid. Melt: solid to liquid.

questions.q: Water drops forming on the outside of a cold glass is called...
questions.explain: Water vapor in the air cools on the cold glass and turns back into liquid drops. That is condensation.
questions.tip: Condensation: a cold can 'sweats' because gas turns into drops.

questions.q: A puddle drying up in the sun is an example of...
questions.explain: The sun warms the water and it turns into water vapor, a gas that floats away into the air.
questions.tip: Evaporation: the water escapes into the air.

questions.q: Which tool measures how much mass an object has?
questions.explain: A balance compares an object with known masses. A ruler measures length and a thermometer measures temperature.
questions.tip: Mass goes on the balance; length goes on the ruler.

questions.q: Which of these is a physical change?
questions.explain: Cut paper is still paper. Burning, baking and rusting make new substances, so those are chemical changes.
questions.tip: Physical change: same stuff, new shape or size.

questions.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
questions.explain: Burning turns wood into ash, smoke and gases: new substances. Melting, tearing and dissolving keep the same substances.
questions.tip: Chemical change: you can't easily get the old stuff back.

questions.q: At what temperature does water freeze?
questions.explain: Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius, which is 32 degrees Fahrenheit, and boils at 100 degrees Celsius (212 Fahrenheit).
questions.tip: Zero is freezing, one hundred is boiling, on the Celsius scale.

questions.q: Sugar stirred into water until you cannot see it anymore makes a...
questions.explain: The sugar dissolves: it spreads out evenly in the water and is still there, which is why the water tastes sweet.
questions.tip: Dissolved sugar is hiding, not gone: taste it!

questions.q: How long does Earth take to spin around once?
questions.explain: One full spin, or rotation, takes about 24 hours. That is one day.
questions.tip: One spin equals one day: 24 hours.

questions.q: How long does Earth take to travel once around the Sun?
questions.explain: One trip around the Sun, called an orbit or revolution, takes about 365 days: one year.
questions.tip: One lap around the Sun is one year, and one birthday.

questions.q: What causes day and night?
questions.explain: As Earth spins, the side facing the Sun has day and the side facing away has night.
questions.tip: Earth spins like a slow top: light side day, dark side night.

questions.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.explain: The order from the Sun is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
questions.tip: My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles: Mercury is first.

questions.q: Which is the largest planet in our solar system?
questions.explain: Jupiter is so big that more than 1,000 Earths could fit inside it.
questions.tip: Jupiter is the giant: J for jumbo.

questions.q: What does the Moon travel around?
questions.explain: The Moon orbits Earth about once a month, and together they orbit the Sun.
questions.tip: The Moon circles us; we circle the Sun.

questions.q: What are the three main types of rock?
questions.explain: Igneous rock cools from melted rock, sedimentary rock forms from layers of pressed sediment, and metamorphic rock is changed by heat and pressure.
questions.tip: Igneous ignites (from fire), sedimentary settles, metamorphic morphs.

questions.q: What is the thin outer layer of Earth that we live on called?
questions.explain: Earth has a crust on the outside, a thick mantle in the middle and a hot core at the center.
questions.tip: Earth is like a peach: skin (crust), flesh (mantle), pit (core).

questions.q: What is a fossil?
choices: The preserved remains or traces of something that lived long ago
questions.explain: Fossils are bones, shells, leaf prints or footprints kept in rock for thousands or millions of years.
questions.tip: A fossil is a message from the past, written in stone.

questions.q: Which planet comes right after Mars, going out from the Sun?
questions.explain: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, then Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
questions.tip: My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles: after Mars comes Jupiter.

questions.q: In the water cycle, which step sends water up into the air as vapor?
questions.explain: The sun evaporates water from oceans and lakes. It condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, and collects in rivers and seas again.
questions.tip: Evaporate up, condense into clouds, precipitate down.

questions.q: What is a hypothesis?
choices: A smart guess you can test
questions.explain: A hypothesis is an idea about what will happen and why, written so you can test it.
questions.tip: Hypothesis: 'I think... because...' and then test it.

questions.q: In a fair test, how many things should you change at a time?
questions.explain: If you change only one thing, you know that thing caused any difference you see.
questions.tip: Change one thing, keep the rest the same.

questions.q: What do scientists do after collecting their results?
choices: Draw a conclusion from the evidence
questions.explain: A conclusion says what the results show and whether the hypothesis was supported.
questions.tip: Results first, then the conclusion.

questions.q: Which tool lets you see something very small, like a tiny bug's leg?
questions.explain: A microscope makes tiny things look big. Micro means small.
questions.tip: MICROscope for MICRO (tiny) things.

questions.q: Which tool helps you see far-away planets and stars?
questions.explain: A telescope gathers light from far away and makes distant objects look closer. Tele means far.
questions.tip: TELEscope for far-away things, like a TELEphone call from far away.

questions.q: What is an observation?
choices: Something you notice with your senses
An opinion about what is pretty
questions.explain: Observations are what you see, hear, smell, feel or measure, like 'the plant grew 3 centimeters'.
questions.tip: Observe: use your senses and write it down.

questions.q: Why do scientists repeat their experiments?
choices: To check that they get the same results again
Because they forgot the first results
To change the answer they got
questions.explain: A result that happens again and again is more trustworthy than one that happened only once.
questions.tip: Once is a fluke, twice is a hint, many times is evidence.

questions.q: What should you write in a science notebook?
choices: What you did and exactly what happened
questions.explain: Writing everything down, even surprises and mistakes, lets you and others understand and repeat the experiment.
questions.tip: If it isn't written down, it didn't happen (in science).

questions.q: You test whether plants grow taller with more water. What is the one thing you should change?
questions.explain: The amount of water is what you are testing, so only that changes. The plants, pots and light stay the same for a fair test.
questions.tip: Testing water? Change only the water.

questions.q: Which part of a cell holds its DNA and acts as its control center?
questions.explain: The nucleus stores the cell's genetic instructions and directs what the cell does.
questions.tip: The nucleus is the cell's brain and library in one.

questions.q: Which organelle releases most of a cell's usable energy from food?
questions.explain: Mitochondria break down sugar with oxygen to make ATP, the energy molecule cells use.
questions.tip: The mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell.

questions.q: Which parts do plant cells have that animal cells do not?
questions.explain: The stiff cell wall gives plants support, and chloroplasts let them make food from sunlight. Animal cells have neither.
questions.tip: Plants are green and stand up straight: chloroplasts and cell walls.

questions.q: Where does photosynthesis happen in a plant cell?
questions.explain: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, the green pigment that captures sunlight to make sugar.
questions.tip: CHLOROplasts hold CHLOROphyll and catch the light.

questions.q: What controls which materials enter and leave a cell?
questions.explain: The cell membrane is a thin, flexible layer that lets some things through and keeps others out.
questions.tip: The membrane is the cell's security gate.

questions.q: Which of these is made of just one cell?
questions.explain: Bacteria are unicellular. Dogs, trees and mushrooms are multicellular: made of many cells working together.
questions.tip: UNI means one: a unicellular bacterium is one cell doing everything.

questions.q: Cells make up tissues, tissues make up organs, and organs make up...
questions.explain: Heart muscle cells form heart tissue, which forms the heart, which is part of the circulatory system.
questions.tip: Cells, tissues, organs, systems: small to big, like bricks, walls, rooms, house.

questions.q: Cell theory says all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and...
choices: All cells come from existing cells
questions.explain: New cells form only when existing cells divide. Cells do not appear from nothing.
questions.tip: Cells come from cells, like puppies come from dogs.

questions.q: What is the jelly-like fluid that fills a cell and holds its parts?
questions.explain: The cytoplasm is mostly water. The organelles float in it, and many chemical reactions happen there.
questions.tip: Cytoplasm: the cell's jelly.

questions.q: A group of the same species living in one area is called a...
questions.explain: All the deer in a forest are a population. All the living things there together are a community.
questions.tip: Population: one species, one place.

questions.q: All the living and nonliving things in an area together make up...
questions.explain: An ecosystem includes the plants and animals plus the water, soil, air and sunlight they depend on.
questions.tip: Ecosystem = everything living and nonliving, working as a system.

questions.q: Which gas do plants take in from the air for photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Plants take in carbon dioxide and water, use light energy to make sugar, and release oxygen.
questions.tip: Plants breathe in what we breathe out: carbon dioxide.

questions.q: About how much of the energy at one level of an energy pyramid passes up to the next level?
questions.explain: Most energy is used for living or lost as heat. Only about a tenth is stored in the body and passed on to whatever eats it.
questions.tip: The 10 percent rule: each step up keeps a dime of every dollar.

questions.q: Bees get nectar from flowers and flowers get pollinated. What is this kind of relationship called?
questions.explain: In mutualism, both species benefit. In parasitism, one benefits and the other is harmed.
questions.tip: MUTUALism: a mutual win-win.

questions.q: Which of these is an abiotic (nonliving) part of an ecosystem?
questions.explain: Abiotic factors include sunlight, water, temperature, soil and air. Biotic factors are the living things.
questions.tip: A-biotic: NOT alive (a means not).

questions.q: What role do most bacteria and fungi play in an ecosystem?
questions.explain: Decomposers break down dead material and waste, returning nutrients to the soil for plants to use.
questions.tip: Decomposers recycle the dead back into dirt.

questions.q: Which biome has long cold winters and forests of evergreen cone-bearing trees?
questions.explain: The taiga stretches across Canada, Scandinavia and Russia. Spruce, fir and pine trees keep their needles through the winter.
questions.tip: Taiga: the snowy pine forest with moose and wolves.

questions.q: Most nitrogen in the air cannot be used by plants directly. What changes it into a usable form?
choices: Bacteria in soil and in plant roots
questions.explain: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria turn nitrogen gas into compounds plants can absorb. This is part of the nitrogen cycle.
questions.tip: Tiny bacteria 'fix' nitrogen so plants can eat it.

questions.q: What is an invasive species?
choices: A species brought to a new place that spreads and harms native species
An animal that is going extinct
questions.explain: Without their usual predators or diseases, invasive species such as kudzu or zebra mussels can crowd out native ones.
questions.tip: Invasive: invades a new home and takes over.

questions.q: A car travels 150 kilometers in 3 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.explain: Speed = distance divided by time: 150 km / 3 h = 50 km/h.
questions.tip: Speed is distance OVER time: put distance on top and divide.

questions.q: Newton's first law: an object keeps doing what it is doing unless acted on by...
questions.explain: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed, until a net force changes that.
questions.tip: First law: lazy objects. They won't change unless pushed.

questions.q: The tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion is called...
questions.explain: Inertia is why you lurch forward when a car stops suddenly: your body keeps moving.
questions.tip: Inertia: 'I'm not changing, you can't make me' (unless a force does).

questions.q: When the forces on an object are balanced, the object...
choices: Keeps the same motion (stays still or moves at a steady speed)
questions.explain: Balanced forces cancel out, so there is no net force and no change in motion.
questions.tip: Balanced forces: tug of war with nobody winning.

questions.q: Which unit measures force?
questions.explain: Force is measured in newtons (N). Mass is in kilograms, length in meters and volume in liters.
questions.tip: Newton's laws, newtons for force.

questions.q: How are mass and weight different?
choices: Weight depends on gravity; mass stays the same everywhere
Mass changes on the Moon; weight does not
They are exactly the same thing
questions.explain: On the Moon your mass is unchanged but your weight is about one sixth, because the Moon's gravity is weaker.
questions.tip: Mass is how much stuff; weight is how hard gravity pulls on it.

questions.q: What is acceleration?
choices: A change in velocity over time (speeding up, slowing down or turning)
questions.explain: Any change in speed or direction is an acceleration, even slowing down (which is sometimes called deceleration).
questions.tip: Accelerate: faster, slower OR a turn all count.

questions.q: Force = mass x acceleration. What force gives a 2 kilogram cart an acceleration of 3 meters per second squared?
questions.explain: F = m x a = 2 x 3 = 6 newtons.
questions.tip: F = ma: multiply, don't add.

questions.q: Why does a box slide farther on a smooth floor than on carpet?
choices: The smooth floor has less friction
Gravity is weaker on smooth floors
questions.explain: Friction opposes sliding. Rougher surfaces make more friction, so they slow the box faster.
questions.tip: Rough rubs, smooth slides.

questions.q: A stretched rubber band stores what kind of energy?
questions.explain: Potential energy is stored energy. The stretched band turns it into kinetic energy (motion) when you let go.
questions.tip: Potential = stored up, waiting. Kinetic = moving now.

questions.q: A moving bicycle has...
questions.explain: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. The faster or heavier the object, the more kinetic energy it has.
questions.tip: Kinetic: think 'kinetic' = 'kicking into motion'.

questions.q: The law of conservation of energy says energy cannot be...
choices: Created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another
questions.explain: The total energy stays the same. A falling ball's potential energy becomes kinetic energy, then heat and sound when it lands.
questions.tip: Energy is never made or lost, it just changes costumes.

questions.q: Heat moving from a hot spoon handle into your hand is...
questions.explain: Conduction is heat passing through direct contact, especially through metals.
questions.tip: Conduction: contact. Touch it and the heat travels.

questions.q: Warm air rising and cooler air sinking to take its place is...
questions.explain: Convection moves heat through a liquid or gas as the warm, less dense part rises.
questions.tip: Convection: currents carry the heat (hot air rises).

questions.q: How does the Sun's heat reach Earth through empty space?
questions.explain: Radiation carries energy as waves (like light and infrared) and needs no material to travel through.
questions.tip: Radiation rays: sunshine on your face is radiation.

questions.q: Which of these is a renewable energy source?
questions.explain: Sunlight, wind, flowing water and plant material are replenished naturally. Coal, oil and gas take millions of years to form.
questions.tip: Renewable: nature keeps re-supplying it (sun, wind, water).

questions.q: A ball sitting at the top of a hill has mostly...
questions.explain: Its height above the ground gives it stored energy that becomes motion if it rolls down.
questions.tip: Up high = potential energy piled up.

questions.q: What energy changes happen in a battery-powered flashlight?
questions.explain: The battery's chemicals push electric current through the bulb, which gives off light (and some heat).
questions.tip: Battery (chemical), wires (electrical), bulb (light).

questions.q: What is the smallest unit of an element that still has that element's properties?
questions.explain: Every element is made of one kind of atom. Gold is gold atoms; oxygen is oxygen atoms.
questions.tip: Atoms are the alphabet; molecules are the words.

questions.q: Which particle in an atom has a positive charge?
questions.explain: Protons are positive, electrons are negative and neutrons are neutral.
questions.tip: PROton is POsitive; NEUtron is NEUtral.

questions.q: Where are the protons and neutrons in an atom?
choices: In the nucleus at the center
questions.explain: The tiny, dense nucleus holds the protons and neutrons. Electrons move around it.
questions.tip: Nucleus: the heavy center; electrons buzz around it.

questions.q: The number of protons in an atom tells you its...
choices: Atomic number, which element it is
questions.explain: Every carbon atom has 6 protons; every oxygen atom has 8. Change the proton count and you have a different element.
questions.tip: Protons are the element's ID number.

questions.q: Water (H2O) is made of hydrogen and oxygen atoms bonded together. Water is...
questions.explain: A compound is two or more elements chemically joined. Its properties differ from its parts: hydrogen and oxygen are gases, water is a liquid.
questions.tip: Compound: elements chemically combined.

questions.q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
questions.explain: Au comes from aurum, the Latin word for gold. Ag (argentum) is silver.
questions.tip: Au: 'Ay, you! Give me gold!'

questions.q: Which of these is an element?
questions.explain: Oxygen is one kind of atom. Water and salt are compounds, and air is a mixture of gases.
questions.tip: If it's on the periodic table, it's an element.

questions.q: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explain: Air is about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen, with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and other gases.
questions.tip: Nitrogen is nearly four fifths of every breath.

questions.q: The periodic table arranges the elements in order of...
questions.explain: Elements are ordered by their number of protons, and elements in the same column have similar properties.
questions.tip: Hydrogen is number 1 because it has 1 proton.

questions.q: Earth's rigid outer shell is broken into large moving pieces called...
questions.explain: The plates float on the hot, slowly flowing mantle and move a few centimeters a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.
questions.tip: Plates move as fast as fingernails grow.

questions.q: Where two plates move apart and new crust forms, like at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, is a...
questions.explain: At divergent boundaries, magma rises to fill the gap and hardens into new ocean floor.
questions.tip: DIverge = DIvide: the plates split apart.

questions.q: The San Andreas Fault in California, where two plates slide past each other, is a...
questions.explain: At transform boundaries the plates grind sideways past each other, causing earthquakes.
questions.tip: Transform: sideways slide, like rubbing your hands together.

questions.q: Which layer of Earth is the hottest?
questions.explain: The inner core is solid iron and nickel at over 5,000 degrees Celsius, kept solid by the enormous pressure.
questions.tip: Deeper is hotter: the core is the hottest.

questions.q: How did the Himalaya mountains form?
choices: Two continental plates collided (India pushed into Asia)
questions.explain: When continents collide, neither sinks, so the crust crumples and rises. The Himalayas are still growing.
questions.tip: Crash two cars and the hoods crumple up: that's mountain building.

questions.q: Where do most earthquakes and volcanoes happen?
questions.explain: The edges of plates are where rock breaks, grinds and melts. The Ring of Fire around the Pacific is the busiest zone.
questions.tip: Plates meet, ground shakes.

questions.q: Who proposed in 1912 that the continents had drifted apart from one supercontinent?
questions.explain: Wegener noticed matching coastlines and fossils on different continents. His idea of continental drift was accepted decades later as plate tectonics.
questions.tip: Wegener: the continents 'wander'.

questions.q: The supercontinent that existed about 250 million years ago is called...
questions.explain: Pangaea means 'all lands'. It slowly broke apart into the continents we know today.
questions.tip: PAN-gaea: pan means all, like a pan-pizza with everything.

questions.q: The Ring of Fire, a belt of volcanoes and earthquakes, surrounds which ocean?
questions.explain: About three quarters of the world's active volcanoes are on the edges of the Pacific plate.
questions.tip: Pacific plate, fiery edges.

questions.q: Which scale rates how hard a mineral is by what it can scratch?
questions.explain: The Mohs scale runs from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond). Richter-type scales measure earthquakes.
questions.tip: Mohs: diamond is a 10, talc is a 1.

questions.q: What is the difference between weather and climate?
choices: Climate is the average weather of a place over many years
Weather is the average over decades
questions.explain: Weather is what happens today; climate is the usual pattern over 30 years or more.
questions.tip: Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get.

questions.q: Which instrument measures air pressure?
questions.explain: Falling pressure often means a storm is coming; rising pressure means fair weather.
questions.tip: BAROmeter: the pressure gauge in the weather forecaster's bag.

questions.q: What does an anemometer measure?
questions.explain: An anemometer has cups that spin in the wind. Faster spinning means faster wind.
questions.tip: ANEMOmeter: the spinning-cup wind tool (anemos is Greek for wind).

questions.q: Which tall, towering cloud brings thunderstorms?
questions.explain: Cumulonimbus clouds can reach over 10 kilometers high. Cirrus are thin and wispy; stratus are flat gray layers.
questions.tip: NIMBUS means rain cloud; cumuloNIMBUS is the thunderhead.

questions.q: What is humidity?
choices: The amount of water vapor in the air
questions.explain: High humidity makes hot days feel muggy because sweat evaporates more slowly.
questions.tip: Humid = heavy with water.

questions.q: A boundary where a cold air mass pushes into warmer air is called a...
questions.explain: Cold fronts often bring a line of thunderstorms followed by cooler, clearer weather.
questions.tip: Cold front: the cold air is out in front, pushing in.

questions.q: Hurricanes get their energy from...
questions.explain: Hurricanes form over tropical oceans warmer than about 26 degrees Celsius and weaken quickly over land or cold water.
questions.tip: Warm sea feeds the storm.

questions.q: In which layer of the atmosphere does almost all weather happen?
questions.explain: The troposphere is the lowest layer, where we live and where clouds, rain and wind occur.
questions.tip: TROPOsphere: the TROPical, stormy bottom layer.

questions.q: What is the greenhouse effect?
choices: Gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapor trapping heat in the atmosphere
questions.explain: Greenhouse gases let sunlight in but slow the escape of heat. Without them Earth would be frozen; more of them makes Earth warmer.
questions.tip: Like a greenhouse: light comes in, heat stays in.

questions.q: Which tool shows the direction the wind is blowing from?
questions.explain: A wind vane (weather vane) turns to point into the wind.
questions.tip: The rooster on the barn roof is a wind vane.

questions.q: In an experiment, the independent variable is...
choices: The one thing the scientist changes on purpose
questions.explain: If you test how fertilizer affects plant height, the amount of fertilizer is the independent variable.
questions.tip: Independent: 'I' change it.

questions.q: The dependent variable is...
choices: What is measured to see the effect
questions.explain: In the fertilizer test, plant height is the dependent variable: it depends on how much fertilizer was used.
questions.tip: Dependent: the Data you collect.

questions.q: What is a control group?
choices: A group that gets no treatment, for comparison
The group that gets the most treatment
questions.explain: Plants given no fertilizer show what happens normally, so you can tell if the fertilizer made a difference.
questions.tip: Control: the 'nothing changed' group to compare against.

questions.q: Things kept the same in every trial of an experiment are called...
questions.explain: Same pots, same soil, same light: keeping these constant makes the test fair.
questions.tip: Constants stay constant.

questions.q: In science, what is a theory?
choices: A well-tested explanation supported by a large body of evidence
Something that has never been checked
questions.explain: The theory of plate tectonics and cell theory are backed by huge amounts of evidence. In science, 'theory' does not mean 'guess'.
questions.tip: Scientific theory: tested, tested, tested, and still standing.

questions.q: Which of these is written as a testable hypothesis?
choices: If plants get more light, then they will grow taller
questions.explain: A good hypothesis predicts a result that an experiment could support or disprove.
questions.tip: If... then...: the hypothesis sandwich.

questions.q: Why do scientists publish their work and let others repeat it?
choices: So other experts can check for mistakes and confirm the results
Because it is required by law
questions.explain: This is peer review and replication. A result that others can reproduce is trustworthy.
questions.tip: Science is a team sport: everyone checks everyone's work.

questions.q: A line graph shows water temperature over time. Which variable goes on the horizontal (x) axis?
questions.explain: The independent variable goes on the x-axis and the measured (dependent) variable on the y-axis.
questions.tip: DRY MIX: Dependent, Responding, Y-axis; Manipulated, Independent, X-axis.

questions.q: What is the shape of a DNA molecule?
questions.explain: DNA is two strands twisted around each other like a spiral staircase, with the base pairs as the steps.
questions.tip: DNA: a twisted ladder.

questions.q: In DNA, adenine (A) always pairs with...
questions.explain: A pairs with T and C pairs with G. In RNA, uracil takes thymine's place.
questions.tip: Apples in Trees, Cars in Garages: A-T, C-G.

questions.q: A dominant allele shows its trait when...
choices: At least one copy is present
Only when two copies are present
questions.explain: One dominant allele masks a recessive one. A recessive trait shows only when both alleles are recessive.
questions.tip: Dominant dominates: one copy is enough.

questions.q: Two parents are both Tt (tall, carrying a recessive short allele). What is the chance a child is tt (short)?
questions.explain: A Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt: one of the four boxes is tt.
questions.tip: Tt x Tt gives 1:2:1, so the double recessive is 1 in 4.

questions.q: Gregor Mendel worked out the basic rules of inheritance by breeding...
questions.explain: In the 1860s Mendel crossed thousands of pea plants and tracked traits like height and seed color.
questions.tip: Mendel and his peas: the father of genetics in a monastery garden.

questions.q: Before a cell divides, its DNA is copied. This is called...
questions.explain: Replication makes a complete copy of the DNA so each new cell gets a full set.
questions.tip: Replicate = make a replica (copy).

questions.q: Which statement best describes natural selection?
choices: Individuals with traits that help them survive and reproduce pass those traits on more often
Organisms choose which traits to develop
Traits gained during life are passed to offspring
questions.explain: Over many generations, helpful inherited traits become more common in a population. This is how populations adapt.
questions.tip: Nature 'selects' the survivors, and survivors have the babies.

questions.q: Charles Darwin studied finches with different beak shapes on which islands?
questions.explain: Darwin visited the Galapagos in 1835 on the HMS Beagle. The finches' beaks matched the food on each island.
questions.tip: Darwin, the Beagle, the Galapagos finches.

questions.q: A mutation is...
choices: A change in the DNA sequence, which may be harmful, helpful or have no effect
questions.explain: Most mutations do nothing noticeable. Some cause disease, and a few give an advantage. Mutations in sex cells can be inherited.
questions.tip: Mutations are typos in the DNA: most harmless, some bad, a few lucky.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are in a normal human body cell?
questions.explain: Body cells have 23 pairs, 46 in all. Egg and sperm cells have 23 each, so the child gets 46.
questions.tip: 23 from Mom plus 23 from Dad equals 46.

questions.q: Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries the instructions from the DNA to the...
questions.explain: DNA stays in the nucleus. mRNA copies a gene and takes it to a ribosome, which reads it to build a protein.
questions.tip: DNA writes the recipe, mRNA delivers it, the ribosome cooks.

questions.q: Mitosis produces...
choices: Four sex cells with half the chromosomes
questions.explain: Mitosis is how you grow and repair tissue: one cell divides into two cells with the same DNA.
questions.tip: MiTOsis makes TWO identical cells.

questions.q: Meiosis produces...
choices: Sex cells (gametes) with half the usual number of chromosomes
questions.explain: Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that when egg and sperm join, the full number is restored.
questions.tip: MEIosis makes 'ME' halves: eggs and sperm.

questions.q: What are the products of photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen.
questions.tip: Plants eat CO2 and water, make sugar, and breathe out oxygen.

questions.q: Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose and produces...
questions.explain: Glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP). It is the reverse of photosynthesis overall.
questions.tip: Respiration runs photosynthesis backwards.

questions.q: Enzymes are...
choices: Proteins that speed up chemical reactions in living things
questions.explain: Each enzyme fits one kind of molecule, like a key in a lock, and is not used up in the reaction.
questions.tip: EnzymeS Speed thingS up.

questions.q: Red blood cells carry oxygen using which protein?
questions.explain: Hemoglobin contains iron, which binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues. It makes blood red.
questions.tip: HEMOglobin: HEMO means blood.

questions.q: Which hormone, made by the pancreas, lowers blood sugar?
questions.explain: Insulin tells cells to take up glucose from the blood. Without enough insulin, blood sugar stays high (diabetes).
questions.tip: Insulin lets sugar IN.

questions.q: Neurons pass signals to the next cell across a tiny gap called a...
questions.explain: At the synapse, the neuron releases chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) that cross the gap.
questions.tip: Synapse: the gap the signal jumps.

questions.q: Homeostasis is...
choices: Keeping the body's internal conditions stable, such as temperature
questions.explain: Sweating when hot and shivering when cold are ways your body keeps its temperature near 37 degrees Celsius.
questions.tip: HomeoSTAsis: STAy the same.

questions.q: Elements in the same column (group) of the periodic table have...
choices: Similar chemical properties, because they have the same number of outer electrons
questions.explain: Lithium, sodium and potassium are all in Group 1, have one outer electron, and all react violently with water.
questions.tip: Same column, same outer electrons, same behavior.

questions.q: Why are the noble gases (helium, neon, argon) so unreactive?
choices: Their outer electron shells are full
questions.explain: Atoms react to fill their outer shell. Noble gases already have a full shell, so they have no reason to bond.
questions.tip: Noble gases are too 'noble' to mix: full shells, no deals.

questions.q: An ionic bond forms when...
choices: One atom transfers electrons to another, as in sodium chloride
questions.explain: Sodium gives an electron to chlorine, making Na+ and Cl- ions that attract each other.
questions.tip: Ionic: one gives, one takes (metal gives to nonmetal).

questions.q: A covalent bond forms when...
choices: Two atoms share a pair of electrons, as in water
questions.explain: Nonmetals usually bond covalently. In H2O each hydrogen shares electrons with oxygen.
questions.tip: CO-valent: CO-operate and share.

questions.q: An atom that loses an electron becomes...
questions.explain: Losing a negative electron leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is positive.
questions.tip: Lose a negative, become positive. CATion is PAWSitive.

questions.q: Isotopes of the same element differ in their number of...
questions.explain: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons, but 6 and 8 neutrons. Same element, different mass.
questions.tip: IsoTOPES: same element, different neutron TOTALS.

questions.q: Carbon-12 has 6 protons. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explain: Mass number = protons + neutrons, so 12 - 6 = 6 neutrons.
questions.tip: Mass number minus protons equals neutrons.

questions.q: Which of these is a halogen?
questions.explain: The halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine) are in Group 17 and need one more electron, so they react strongly with metals.
questions.tip: Halogens: the salt-formers, one electron short.

questions.q: Metals tend to...
questions.explain: Metal atoms hold their outer electrons loosely, which is why they form positive ions and let current flow.
questions.tip: Metals are generous: they give electrons away.

questions.q: Group 1 metals such as sodium and potassium react with water...
questions.explain: Alkali metals react so strongly with water that potassium bursts into flame. They are stored under oil.
questions.tip: Alkali metals in water: fizz, pop, flame!

questions.q: The law of conservation of mass says that in a chemical reaction...
choices: The total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants
Mass is always lost as heat
questions.explain: Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, so a balanced equation has the same atoms on both sides.
questions.tip: Atoms in equals atoms out.

questions.q: In 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, how many water molecules form from two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule?
questions.explain: The coefficient 2 in front of H2O means two water molecules. Count the atoms: 4 H and 2 O on each side.
questions.tip: The big number in front counts molecules.

questions.q: Lemon juice has a pH of about 2. It is...
questions.explain: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral (pure water) and above 7 is basic.
questions.tip: Low pH, sour and acidic; 7 is neutral water.

questions.q: An exothermic reaction...
questions.explain: Burning wood and hand warmers are exothermic. Endothermic reactions, like an instant cold pack, absorb heat.
questions.tip: EXOthermic: heat EXits.

questions.q: A catalyst...
choices: Speeds up a reaction without being used up
Is used up in the reaction
questions.explain: Catalysts lower the energy needed to start a reaction. Enzymes are the body's catalysts.
questions.tip: A catalyst is a helper that walks away unchanged.

questions.q: Which change usually makes a reaction go faster?
choices: Using bigger solid chunks instead of powder
questions.explain: Hotter particles move faster and collide more often and harder, so more collisions lead to a reaction.
questions.tip: Hot and crowded means fast: more collisions.

questions.q: When an acid reacts with a base, the products are...
questions.explain: This is neutralization: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide -> sodium chloride (table salt) + water.
questions.tip: Acid + base = salt + water, and the pH heads toward 7.

questions.q: Iron rusting is an example of...
questions.explain: Rust is iron oxide. Water speeds it up, which is why wet iron rusts faster.
questions.tip: Rust: iron plus oxygen, slowly 'burning'.

questions.q: In 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl, the sodium and chlorine are the...
questions.explain: Reactants are on the left of the arrow and products on the right.
questions.tip: Reactants react; the arrow points to the products.

questions.q: One mole of any substance contains about how many particles?
questions.explain: This is Avogadro's number. One mole of carbon-12 atoms weighs 12 grams.
questions.tip: Avogadro's number: 6.02 x 10^23, so chemists celebrate Mole Day on 10/23 at 6:02.

questions.q: Newton's third law says that for every action force there is...
choices: An equal and opposite reaction force
questions.explain: A rocket pushes exhaust gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up with equal force.
questions.tip: Push the wall, the wall pushes back.

questions.q: A net force of 20 newtons acts on a 10 kilogram box. Its acceleration is...
questions.explain: Newton's second law: a = F / m = 20 / 10 = 2 m/s^2.
questions.tip: F = ma, so a = F over m.

questions.q: Near Earth's surface, the acceleration due to gravity is about...
questions.explain: A falling object (ignoring air) gains about 9.8 m/s of speed every second.
questions.tip: Gravity's number: 9.8 (call it 10 for quick estimates).

questions.q: Kinetic energy is one half times mass times velocity squared. If a car's speed doubles, its kinetic energy...
questions.explain: KE depends on velocity squared: 2 squared is 4. That is why a crash at twice the speed is far worse.
questions.tip: Double the speed, four times the energy.

questions.q: Work equals force times distance. Lifting a 10 newton book up 2 meters does how much work?
questions.explain: W = F x d = 10 N x 2 m = 20 joules.
questions.tip: Work: force times distance, measured in joules.

questions.q: Momentum is...
questions.explain: A heavy truck moving slowly can have as much momentum as a light car moving fast. Units are kilogram meters per second.
questions.tip: Momentum: p = mv (p for 'push-through').

questions.q: Power is the rate of doing work. Its unit, the watt, equals...
questions.explain: A 60 watt bulb uses 60 joules of energy every second.
questions.tip: Watts = joules per second: how fast energy is used.

questions.q: A feather and a hammer are dropped together in a vacuum. What happens?
choices: They hit the ground at the same time
questions.explain: Without air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration. Apollo 15 astronauts showed this on the Moon in 1971.
questions.tip: No air, no difference: everything falls alike.

questions.q: A ball is dropped from rest (ignore air). After one second, about how fast is it moving?
questions.explain: Speed = acceleration x time = 9.8 x 1 = 9.8 m/s.
questions.tip: Each second of falling adds about 9.8 m/s.

questions.q: Why can sound not travel through empty space?
choices: Sound needs a material (a medium) to travel through
questions.explain: Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle. With no particles, there is nothing to vibrate. Light does not need a medium.
questions.tip: In space, no one can hear you scream: no air, no sound.

questions.q: The speed of light in a vacuum is about...
questions.explain: Light could circle Earth about seven times in one second. Sound in air is only about 340 meters per second.
questions.tip: Light: 300,000 km every second. Nothing is faster.

questions.q: Wave speed equals...
questions.explain: If 10 waves pass per second (10 Hz) and each is 2 meters long, the wave moves 20 meters per second.
questions.tip: v = f times lambda: how many waves per second, times how long each is.

questions.q: A sound with a higher frequency has a...
questions.explain: Frequency sets pitch; amplitude sets loudness. A violin's high notes vibrate faster than a cello's low notes.
questions.tip: Fast vibrations, high notes.

questions.q: Light bending as it passes from air into water is called...
questions.explain: Light slows down in water and changes direction, which is why a straw in a glass looks bent.
questions.tip: ReFRACTion bends (FRACTures the path); reflection bounces.

questions.q: Ohm's law is V = I x R. A 12 volt battery across a 4 ohm resistor gives a current of...
questions.explain: I = V / R = 12 / 4 = 3 amps.
questions.tip: V equals I R: cover the one you want (I = V over R).

questions.q: Which has the longest wavelength in the electromagnetic spectrum?
questions.explain: From longest to shortest: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
questions.tip: Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns: radio to gamma, long to short.

questions.q: In a series circuit, if one bulb burns out...
choices: All the bulbs go out, because the only path is broken
questions.explain: A series circuit has one path. In a parallel circuit each bulb has its own path, so the others keep working.
questions.tip: Series: one road, one roadblock stops everything.

questions.q: An electric current in a metal wire is a flow of...
questions.explain: The loosely held outer electrons in a metal drift through the wire when a voltage pushes them.
questions.tip: Electricity = electrons on the move.

questions.q: The unit of electrical resistance is the...
questions.explain: Resistance (ohms) is how much a material opposes current. Volts push, amps flow, watts measure power.
questions.tip: Volts push, amps flow, ohms resist.

questions.q: Outside a bar magnet, the magnetic field lines run from...
choices: The north pole to the south pole
The south pole to the north pole
Nowhere, there are no lines outside
questions.explain: Field lines leave the north pole, curve around, and enter the south pole. Opposite poles attract, like poles repel.
questions.tip: North out, south in.

questions.q: About how old is Earth?
questions.explain: Radiometric dating of meteorites and the oldest rocks gives about 4.54 billion years. The universe is older, about 13.8 billion.
questions.tip: Earth: four and a half billion. Universe: nearly fourteen billion.

questions.q: Sedimentary rock forms from...
choices: Layers of sediment pressed and cemented together
Rock changed by heat and pressure
questions.explain: Sandstone, limestone and shale form as sand, shells and mud pile up over millions of years. Most fossils are found in them.
questions.tip: Sediment settles, layer on layer, then hardens.

questions.q: Which of these is a metamorphic rock?
questions.explain: Marble is limestone changed by heat and pressure. Granite and basalt are igneous; sandstone is sedimentary.
questions.tip: Marble was limestone that got 'cooked' underground.

questions.q: What causes Earth's seasons?
choices: The tilt of Earth's axis as it orbits the Sun
Earth being closer to the Sun in summer
Changes in how fast Earth spins
questions.explain: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees. When your hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, it gets more direct light and longer days.
questions.tip: Tilt, not distance: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.

questions.q: Ocean tides are caused mainly by...
questions.explain: The Moon's pull makes the oceans bulge, giving most coasts two high tides a day. The Sun adds a smaller effect.
questions.tip: The Moon tugs the tides.

questions.q: The ozone layer in the stratosphere protects life by absorbing...
questions.explain: Ozone (O3) soaks up most of the Sun's harmful UV. The 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out the chemicals that were thinning it.
questions.tip: Ozone: Earth's sunscreen.

questions.q: Carbon-14 dating works for...
choices: Things that were once alive, up to about 50,000 years old
questions.explain: Living things take in carbon-14; after death it decays with a half-life of about 5,730 years. Older rocks need other isotopes like uranium.
questions.tip: Carbon-14 for bones and wood; uranium for ancient rocks.

questions.q: When the Moon is between Earth and the Sun and its lit side faces away from us, the phase is...
questions.explain: At new moon we see the dark side, so the Moon seems to vanish. At full moon, Earth is between the Sun and Moon.
questions.tip: New moon: nothing to see; full moon: fully lit.

questions.q: The Milky Way is a...
choices: Spiral galaxy containing our solar system
questions.explain: The Milky Way holds hundreds of billions of stars. The Sun is in one of its spiral arms.
questions.tip: The milky band in the night sky is our own galaxy seen edge-on.

questions.q: A solar eclipse happens when...
choices: The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth
Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon
questions.explain: The Moon's shadow falls on Earth. In a lunar eclipse it is the other way around: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
questions.tip: SOLAR eclipse: the Moon blocks the SUN.

questions.q: Which are the four major classes of biological macromolecules?
choices: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids
questions.explain: Carbohydrates store energy and build structures, lipids form membranes and store energy, proteins do most of the cell's work, and nucleic acids (DNA, RNA) carry information.
questions.tip: CLPN: Carbs, Lipids, Proteins, Nucleic acids, 'Cells Love Protein Now'.

questions.q: Proteins are chains of...
questions.explain: There are 20 standard amino acids. The order in which they are linked determines how the protein folds and works.
questions.tip: Amino acids are the beads; a protein is the necklace.

questions.q: The bond that links two amino acids in a protein is a...
questions.explain: A peptide bond forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, releasing water.
questions.tip: Peptide bonds make polypeptides.

questions.q: Cells get energy from ATP when...
choices: ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP and phosphate
ADP is built up into ATP
ATP is stored in the nucleus
questions.explain: Removing the terminal phosphate from ATP releases free energy that drives muscle contraction, transport and synthesis.
questions.tip: ATP is the cell's rechargeable battery: ATP to ADP spends it, ADP to ATP recharges.

questions.q: Where in the cell does glycolysis take place?
questions.explain: Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules in the cytosol, with a net gain of 2 ATP, and needs no oxygen.
questions.tip: Glycolysis: 'glucose lysis', the first step, out in the cytosol.

questions.q: The citric acid (Krebs) cycle takes place in the...
questions.explain: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion, is converted to acetyl-CoA, and the cycle strips off electrons (as NADH and FADH2) and releases CO2.
questions.tip: Krebs in the matrix, deep inside the mitochondrion.

questions.q: In the electron transport chain, the final electron acceptor is...
questions.explain: Electrons end up on oxygen, forming water. That is why we must breathe oxygen: without it the chain stops and ATP production collapses.
questions.tip: Oxygen is the last stop; the electrons plus oxygen make water.

questions.q: Why do most enzymes stop working at high temperature?
questions.explain: Heat breaks the weak bonds that hold the protein's shape, so the active site no longer fits its substrate. Cooking an egg white is denaturation you can see.
questions.tip: Denature = de-shape. No shape, no work.

questions.q: In the central dogma (DNA to RNA to protein), which step is translation?
questions.explain: Transcription copies DNA into mRNA; translation reads the mRNA codons at the ribosome to assemble amino acids.
questions.tip: TRANSCRIBE copies the script (DNA to RNA); TRANSLATE changes the language (RNA to protein).

questions.q: Phospholipids form a bilayer in cell membranes because...
choices: Their heads are hydrophilic and their tails are hydrophobic
They are covalently bonded to each other
questions.explain: The water-loving heads face the watery inside and outside of the cell, and the water-fearing tails hide in the middle.
questions.tip: Heads out to the water, tails tucked in: a lipid sandwich.

questions.q: The overall three-dimensional fold of a single polypeptide chain is its...
questions.explain: Primary is the amino acid sequence, secondary is local helices and sheets, tertiary is the whole chain's fold, and quaternary is several chains together.
questions.tip: 1 sequence, 2 helices and sheets, 3 the full fold, 4 multiple chains.

questions.q: The first law of thermodynamics states that...
choices: The internal energy of a system changes by the heat added minus the work it does
Heat flows from cold to hot
Energy can be created in a closed system
questions.explain: Delta U = Q - W. It is the law of conservation of energy applied to heat and work.
questions.tip: First law: you can't win (no free energy).

questions.q: The second law of thermodynamics says that the total entropy of an isolated system...
questions.explain: Natural processes move toward more disorder overall. Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never the reverse without work.
questions.tip: Second law: you can't break even (entropy wins).

questions.q: Absolute zero, 0 kelvin, is equal to...
questions.explain: At absolute zero, particles have the minimum possible energy. It is about -459.67 degrees Fahrenheit.
questions.tip: Kelvin = Celsius + 273.15; zero kelvin is as cold as it gets.

questions.q: A reaction is spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure when its Gibbs free energy change is...
questions.explain: Delta G = Delta H - T Delta S. A negative Delta G means the process can happen on its own, though it may be slow.
questions.tip: Negative G means Go.

questions.q: A Carnot engine runs between 600 K and 300 K. Its maximum efficiency is...
questions.explain: Efficiency = 1 - Tcold / Thot = 1 - 300/600 = 0.5. No real engine can beat this limit.
questions.tip: Carnot: one minus cold over hot, in kelvin.

questions.q: The specific heat of water is about 4.18 joules per gram per degree Celsius. Heating 100 grams of water by 10 degrees takes about...
questions.explain: Q = m c Delta T = 100 x 4.18 x 10 = 4,180 J. Water's high specific heat is why oceans moderate climate.
questions.tip: Q = m c delta T: mass, specific heat, temperature change, multiply.

questions.q: For an ideal gas at constant volume, doubling the absolute temperature...
questions.explain: PV = nRT: with V and n fixed, P is proportional to T (in kelvin). A sealed can heated in a fire can burst.
questions.tip: PV = nRT: fix V, and P rises with T.

questions.q: While ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius, the heat you add...
choices: Goes into breaking the crystal structure, and the temperature stays at 0
Turns the ice straight to steam
questions.explain: This is latent heat of fusion: about 334 joules per gram for water. Temperature rises again only once all the ice is liquid.
questions.tip: During a phase change the thermometer pauses.

questions.q: The third law of thermodynamics says the entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero is...
questions.explain: At 0 K a perfect crystal has only one possible arrangement, so there is no disorder.
questions.tip: Third law: you can't get out of the game (0 K is unreachable, and there entropy is 0).

questions.q: A process carried out at constant temperature is called...
questions.explain: Iso means same: isothermal (temperature), isobaric (pressure), isochoric (volume). Adiabatic means no heat exchanged.
questions.tip: ISO-THERMAL: same temperature.

questions.q: By Coulomb's law, if the distance between two charges doubles, the force between them...
questions.explain: Electric force is proportional to 1 over distance squared, like gravity. Twice the distance means 2 squared = 4 times weaker.
questions.tip: Inverse square: double the distance, quarter the force.

questions.q: Faraday's law of induction says a voltage (EMF) is induced in a loop when...
choices: The magnetic flux through the loop changes
A steady magnetic field passes through it
The loop is made of plastic
questions.explain: Moving a magnet into or out of a coil, or changing the field strength, induces a current. This is how generators work.
questions.tip: Change the flux, get a volt.

questions.q: Lenz's law says the induced current flows in a direction that...
choices: Opposes the change in flux that caused it
Is always toward the north pole
questions.explain: This is why a magnet dropped through a copper pipe falls slowly: the induced currents push back on it.
questions.tip: Nature resists change: Lenz's law is induction's stubborn streak.

questions.q: A capacitor stores energy in...
choices: An electric field between its plates
A magnetic field in a coil
questions.explain: Capacitance C = Q/V. The stored energy is one half C V squared. Inductors store energy in magnetic fields; batteries store it chemically.
questions.tip: Capacitor: two plates, an electric field, and charge waiting to go.

questions.q: The magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire forms...
choices: Lines pointing away from the wire
questions.explain: Right-hand rule: point your thumb along the current and your fingers curl in the direction of the field.
questions.tip: Thumb is current, fingers curl the way the field goes.

questions.q: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields are...
choices: Perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel
Both along the direction of travel
questions.explain: Light, radio and X-rays are all EM waves: oscillating E and B fields at right angles, moving at c with no medium needed.
questions.tip: E, B and travel direction: three right angles, like the corner of a box.

questions.q: A step-up transformer...
choices: Increases voltage and works only with alternating current
questions.explain: Transformers rely on changing flux, so they need AC. More turns on the secondary coil raise the voltage while the current falls, keeping power the same.
