questions.tip: Transformers need AC: a steady DC field induces nothing.

questions.q: Two 4 ohm resistors connected in parallel have a combined resistance of...
questions.explain: 1/R = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2, so R = 2 ohms. Parallel paths make it easier for current to flow.
questions.tip: Parallel: more paths, less resistance (two equal ones halve it).

questions.q: Gauss's law relates the electric flux through a closed surface to...
choices: The charge enclosed by the surface
questions.explain: Flux = enclosed charge divided by the permittivity of free space. It is one of Maxwell's four equations.
questions.tip: Gauss: count the charge inside the bubble.

questions.q: How many equations make up Maxwell's equations of electromagnetism?
questions.explain: Gauss's law for electricity, Gauss's law for magnetism, Faraday's law and the Ampere-Maxwell law together describe all classical electromagnetism and predict light.
questions.tip: Maxwell's four: two Gauss, one Faraday, one Ampere.

questions.q: How many covalent bonds does a carbon atom normally form?
questions.explain: Carbon has four outer electrons and completes its octet by sharing four more. This lets it build chains, rings and branches.
questions.tip: Carbon has four hands to hold.

questions.q: What is the molecular formula of propane, the three-carbon alkane?
questions.explain: Alkanes follow CnH2n+2. For n = 3: 2 x 3 + 2 = 8 hydrogens.
questions.tip: Alkanes: CnH(2n+2). Meth, eth, prop, but: 1, 2, 3, 4 carbons.

questions.q: Alkenes are hydrocarbons that contain...
choices: At least one carbon-carbon double bond
questions.explain: Ethene (ethylene), C2H4, is the simplest alkene. The double bond makes alkenes more reactive than alkanes.
questions.tip: Alk-ENE has a double bond; alk-ANE is all single; alk-YNE has a triple.

questions.q: A molecule with an -OH group bonded to a carbon chain is an...
questions.explain: Ethanol, CH3CH2OH, is the alcohol in drinks and hand sanitizer.
questions.tip: OH, it's an alcohol.

questions.q: The -COOH functional group identifies a...
questions.explain: Acetic acid (vinegar) is CH3COOH. The carboxyl group gives up a proton, which makes these compounds acidic.
questions.tip: COOH: Carboxylic acids make vinegar sour.

questions.q: Isomers are compounds that have...
choices: The same molecular formula but different structures
Different formulas but the same name
questions.explain: Butane and isobutane are both C4H10 but have different shapes and boiling points.
questions.tip: ISOmers: same ingredients, different recipe.

questions.q: Benzene, C6H6, is...
choices: A flat six-carbon ring with delocalized electrons (aromatic)
A straight chain of six carbons
questions.explain: Benzene's ring shares its electrons evenly around all six carbons, which makes it unusually stable.
questions.tip: Benzene: the hexagon with a circle inside.

questions.q: An ester forms when a carboxylic acid reacts with...
questions.explain: The reaction releases water. Many esters have fruity smells and are used as flavorings.
questions.tip: Acid + alcohol = ester, and esters smell like fruit.

questions.q: A carbon atom is a chiral center when it is bonded to...
questions.explain: A chiral molecule and its mirror image cannot be superimposed, like left and right hands. The two forms can act differently in the body.
questions.tip: Chiral comes from the Greek for hand: left and right versions.

questions.q: The difference between an aldehyde and a ketone is that in an aldehyde the carbonyl (C=O) group is...
choices: At the end of the carbon chain
In the middle of the chain
questions.explain: Formaldehyde and acetaldehyde have the C=O at a chain end, with a hydrogen attached. Acetone, a ketone, has it between two carbons.
questions.tip: Aldehyde at the end, ketone in the middle.

questions.q: Polyethylene, the plastic in bags and bottles, is made by linking many molecules of...
questions.explain: The double bonds of ethene open up and join into long chains. A polymer is many monomers linked together.
questions.tip: POLY-ethylene: many ethylenes in a chain.

questions.q: What is the mean of 2, 4, 6 and 8?
questions.explain: Add them (20) and divide by how many there are (4).
questions.tip: Mean: add them all, divide by the count.

questions.q: What is the median of 3, 9, 1, 7 and 5?
questions.explain: Sort them: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. The middle value is 5. The median is less affected by extreme values than the mean.
questions.tip: Median: line them up and pick the middle.

questions.q: The standard deviation of a data set measures...
choices: How spread out the values are around the mean
questions.explain: A small standard deviation means the values cluster near the mean; a large one means they are widely scattered.
questions.tip: Standard deviation: the typical distance from the mean.

questions.q: A result with p < 0.05 is usually described as...
choices: Statistically significant: unlikely to be due to chance alone if there were no real effect
questions.explain: The p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. 0.05 is a convention, not a law.
questions.tip: Small p, surprising result (if nothing were going on).

questions.q: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer. This shows that...
choices: Correlation does not prove causation; a third factor (hot weather) explains both
questions.explain: A confounding variable, warm weather, drives both. Correlation can point to a cause, but experiments are needed to show it.
questions.tip: Correlation is not causation: look for the hidden third thing.

questions.q: Increasing the sample size of a study generally...
choices: Makes the estimate more precise (smaller standard error)
questions.explain: The standard error shrinks in proportion to the square root of the sample size: four times the data halves the error.
questions.tip: More data, less noise (but four times the data only halves the error).

questions.q: In a double-blind trial...
choices: Neither the participants nor the researchers assessing them know who got the real treatment
Two treatments are compared without a placebo
questions.explain: Blinding prevents expectations from biasing how people report or measure outcomes.
questions.tip: Double-blind: both sides in the dark until the code is broken.

questions.q: In a normal (bell-shaped) distribution, about what fraction of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explain: The 68-95-99.7 rule: 68 percent within one standard deviation, 95 within two, 99.7 within three.
questions.tip: 68, 95, 99.7: one, two, three standard deviations.

questions.q: The null hypothesis in a study usually states that...
choices: There is no effect or no difference
questions.explain: Researchers try to collect evidence against the null hypothesis. Failing to reject it is not the same as proving there is no effect.
questions.tip: Null = nothing going on.

questions.q: How many significant figures does 0.00450 have?
questions.explain: Leading zeros are placeholders and do not count; the trailing zero after the 5 does count because it shows the measurement's precision.
questions.tip: Leading zeros never count; trailing zeros after a decimal point do.

questions.q: Randomly assigning participants to treatment and control groups is done to...
choices: Spread confounding factors evenly so differences are due to the treatment
questions.explain: Randomization means age, health, habits and unknown factors are balanced on average between groups.
questions.tip: Randomize to make the groups twins (on average).

questions.q: A light-year is a unit of...
choices: Distance: how far light travels in one year
Time: one year on a spacecraft
questions.explain: One light-year is about 9.46 trillion kilometers. Looking at distant objects means seeing their past.
questions.tip: Light-YEAR sounds like time, but it measures distance.

questions.q: After the Sun, the nearest star to Earth is...
questions.explain: Proxima Centauri is a small red dwarf in the Alpha Centauri system. Today's fastest spacecraft would take tens of thousands of years to reach it.
questions.tip: PROXIMA means nearest.

questions.q: Stars on the main sequence shine by fusing...
questions.explain: In the core, four hydrogen nuclei become one helium nucleus, and the lost mass becomes energy (E = mc^2).
questions.tip: Main sequence stars are hydrogen burners.

questions.q: What will happen to the Sun in about 5 billion years?
choices: It will swell into a red giant, then shed its outer layers and become a white dwarf
It will explode as a supernova
It will collapse into a black hole
It will become a neutron star
questions.explain: Only stars much more massive than the Sun end as supernovae, neutron stars or black holes.
questions.tip: Sun-sized star: red giant, then white dwarf. Big stars go boom.

questions.q: Hubble's law says that more distant galaxies...
choices: Move away from us faster, showing the universe is expanding
Are always older than nearby ones
questions.explain: Edwin Hubble found in 1929 that a galaxy's redshift grows with its distance. Space itself is stretching.
questions.tip: Farther means faster away: the expanding universe.

questions.q: The age of the universe is about...
questions.explain: Measurements of the cosmic microwave background and the expansion rate agree on roughly 13.8 billion years.
questions.tip: Universe: 13.8 billion. Earth: 4.5 billion.

questions.q: Kepler's first law says planets move in...
choices: Ellipses, with the Sun at one focus
questions.explain: Orbits are slightly stretched circles. His third law adds that the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the orbit's size.
questions.tip: Kepler: ellipses, equal areas, and T squared goes with a cubed.

questions.q: The cosmic microwave background is...
choices: Leftover radiation from the early universe, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang
questions.explain: It is the afterglow of the hot early universe, now cooled to about 2.7 kelvin and coming from every direction.
questions.tip: The CMB is the Big Bang's baby picture.

questions.q: Light from a galaxy is redshifted. This tells us the galaxy is...
questions.explain: A receding source has its light stretched to longer, redder wavelengths (a Doppler-like shift; for distant galaxies it is the expansion of space itself doing the stretching). Approaching sources are blueshifted.
questions.tip: Red means receding.

questions.q: The escape velocity from Earth's surface is about...
questions.explain: An object launched at this speed, ignoring air, would never fall back. Rockets reach it gradually while climbing.
questions.tip: Eleven-ish kilometers per second to leave Earth for good.

questions.q: In 2006, Pluto was reclassified as a...
questions.explain: The International Astronomical Union ruled that a planet must clear its orbit of other objects. Pluto shares the Kuiper Belt with many others.
questions.tip: Pluto got demoted to dwarf planet in 2006.

questions.q: A Hertzsprung-Russell diagram plots stars by their...
questions.explain: Most stars fall along the diagonal main sequence; giants sit at the top right and white dwarfs at the bottom left.
questions.tip: H-R diagram: bright at the top, hot on the left.

questions.q: How does a vaccine protect you?
choices: It shows your immune system a harmless piece or form of a germ so it makes antibodies and memory cells in advance
It kills germs already in your body like an antibiotic
It coats your cells so germs cannot touch them
It replaces your white blood cells
questions.explain: When the real germ shows up later, the immune system recognizes it and responds fast, often before you feel sick.
questions.tip: A vaccine is a wanted poster: the immune system learns the face before the crook arrives.

questions.q: Why don't antibiotics help with a cold or the flu?
choices: Colds and flu are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only work on bacteria
questions.explain: Antibiotics attack structures that bacteria have and viruses do not. Taking them when they are not needed breeds resistant bacteria.
questions.tip: Antibiotics are for bacteria. Viruses just shrug.

questions.q: The 'Calorie' on a food label is...
questions.explain: A food Calorie is 1,000 small calories, or about 4.2 kilojoules. All three macronutrients supply Calories.
questions.tip: Calories are energy, not a kind of food.

questions.q: Which nutrient supplies the most Calories per gram?
questions.explain: Fat has more than twice the energy of carbohydrate or protein by weight. Fiber passes through mostly undigested.
questions.tip: Fat: 9. Carbs and protein: 4 each.

questions.q: Dietary fiber is...
choices: Plant material your body cannot digest, which helps digestion and fullness
questions.explain: Fiber comes from whole grains, beans, fruit and vegetables. It feeds gut bacteria and keeps things moving.
questions.tip: Fiber: the part of plants you can't digest but your gut loves anyway.

questions.q: Your skin makes vitamin D when exposed to...
questions.explain: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones. It is also in oily fish and fortified milk.
questions.tip: Vitamin D is the sunshine vitamin.

questions.q: About how much of an adult's body weight is water?
questions.explain: Water is in every cell and in blood. Losing just a few percent of it causes thirst, headache and tiredness.
questions.tip: You are more than half water.

questions.q: Why does your body produce a fever?
choices: A higher temperature helps the immune system fight infection
The germs heat you up directly
It is a mistake with no purpose
questions.explain: Fever is a deliberate response: many germs reproduce more slowly at higher temperatures and immune cells work faster.
questions.tip: A fever is the body turning up the heat on invaders.

questions.q: What causes sunburn?
questions.explain: You can burn on a cool, cloudy day because UV passes through clouds. Sunscreen and shade block UV, not heat.
questions.tip: It's the UV, not the warmth: you can burn when it's cold.

questions.q: What is herd immunity?
choices: When enough people are immune that a disease has trouble spreading, which protects those who cannot be vaccinated
When a whole family catches the same illness
Immunity that animals pass to people
questions.explain: If most people a germ meets are immune, chains of infection break. The share needed depends on how contagious the disease is.
questions.tip: Herd immunity: the immune crowd shields the few who can't be.

questions.q: Why is the sky blue?
choices: Air molecules scatter blue light more than red light
Blue light comes from the Moon
questions.explain: This is Rayleigh scattering: shorter wavelengths scatter more, so blue light bounces around the sky and reaches your eyes from all directions.
questions.tip: Blue light bounces best, so the whole sky glows blue.

questions.q: Why are sunsets red and orange?
choices: Sunlight passes through much more air near the horizon, and the blue is scattered away before it reaches you
The Sun gets hotter in the evening
The Sun's surface cools in the evening
The Sun is farther away at sunset
questions.explain: The same scattering that makes the sky blue removes the blue from the long path at sunset, leaving the reds.
questions.tip: Sunset: the blue got lost on the long way through the air.

questions.q: Why does ice float on water?
choices: Ice is less dense than liquid water because its molecules lock into an open crystal structure
Ice is lighter because it is colder
Air bubbles always form in ice
Ice is pushed up by the cold
questions.explain: Most substances shrink when they freeze; water expands by about 9 percent. That is why pipes burst and lakes freeze from the top.
questions.tip: Water is weird: it expands when it freezes, so ice floats.

questions.q: How does a microwave oven heat food?
choices: Microwaves make water molecules in the food rotate rapidly, which heats it
It heats the air, which heats the food
It heats the plate, which heats the food
questions.explain: Water molecules are polar, so the oscillating field twists them back and forth billions of times a second. Dry plates stay cool.
questions.tip: Microwaves shake the water, and the water heats the food.

questions.q: Why do you see lightning before you hear its thunder?
choices: Light travels almost instantly; sound takes about 3 seconds per kilometer (5 seconds per mile)
Your eyes are faster than your ears
questions.explain: Count the seconds between flash and thunder and divide by 5 for the distance in miles (by 3 for kilometers).
questions.tip: Flash to boom: count the seconds, divide by five for miles.

questions.q: Why does a straw in a glass of water look bent?
choices: Light changes direction (refracts) as it passes between water and air
The water bends the straw slightly
questions.explain: Light slows down in water. Rays from the submerged part reach your eye from a shifted direction, so the straw looks broken at the surface.
questions.tip: Refraction: light takes a turn at the water's edge.

questions.q: Why does a hot-air balloon rise?
choices: Hot air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it floats up
Hot air pushes against the ground
The flame creates lift like a jet
The balloon fabric is lighter than air
questions.explain: Heating the air makes its molecules spread out, so the balloon and its air weigh less than the air they displace. Same reason a cork floats.
questions.tip: Hot air rises: the balloon is a bubble of warm air in a sea of cool air.

questions.q: Why does spreading salt melt ice on a road?
choices: Salt lowers the freezing point of water, so ice melts below 0 degrees Celsius
questions.explain: Dissolved salt interferes with water forming ice crystals. Below about -10 to -20 degrees Celsius, ordinary salt stops working.
questions.tip: Salt makes water stay liquid at colder temperatures.

questions.q: At the same room temperature, why does a metal doorknob feel colder than a wooden door?
choices: Metal conducts heat away from your hand much faster
questions.explain: Your skin senses heat flow, not temperature. Metal pulls heat out of your hand quickly, so it feels cold even though both are at the same temperature.
questions.tip: You feel heat leaving, not temperature: metal is a fast heat thief.

questions.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
choices: The Moon spins once for every orbit around Earth, so one side always faces us
The Moon does not spin at all
The far side is always dark
Earth's shadow hides the other side
questions.explain: This is tidal locking. The far side gets just as much sunlight as the near side; it is 'far', not 'dark'.
questions.tip: The Moon turns in step with its orbit, like walking around a table while always facing it.

questions.q: How does a gasoline car engine turn fuel into motion?
choices: Fuel and air burn inside cylinders, and the expanding gas pushes pistons that turn the crankshaft
Burning fuel heats water into steam that spins a turbine
The fuel is turned into electricity first
questions.explain: The four strokes are intake, compression, power and exhaust. Thousands of small explosions a minute keep the crankshaft spinning.
questions.tip: Suck, squeeze, bang, blow: the four strokes.

questions.q: How does a battery make electricity?
choices: Chemical reactions inside it push electrons out of one terminal and through the circuit to the other
It stores electricity like water in a tank
It pulls electricity from the air
questions.explain: In a rechargeable lithium-ion battery, charging reverses the reactions by moving lithium ions back to the other electrode.
questions.tip: A battery is a chemical pump for electrons.

questions.q: Wi-Fi sends data using...
choices: Radio waves, mostly around 2.4 and 5 gigahertz
Sound waves too high to hear
Tiny electric currents through the air
questions.explain: The router and your device encode data on radio waves, the same kind of waves as FM radio but at higher frequencies and over short distances.
questions.tip: Wi-Fi is just radio: no wires, just waves.

questions.q: How does a GPS receiver work out where you are?
choices: It times signals from several satellites and uses the differences to calculate its position
It sends your location to the satellites
questions.explain: Each satellite broadcasts the time and its position. With signals from at least four satellites, the receiver solves for its own location and clock error. The satellites never hear from you.
questions.tip: GPS listens, it never talks: it times the satellites' clocks.

questions.q: How does a refrigerator keep food cold?
choices: A refrigerant absorbs heat inside as it evaporates and releases it outside as it is compressed and condensed
It makes cold and stores it
A fan blows the heat out the back
questions.explain: A fridge does not create cold; it moves heat from inside to the coils at the back. That is why the back feels warm. Air conditioners work the same way.
questions.tip: A fridge is a heat pump: it pumps heat out, it doesn't make cold.

questions.q: Why do LED bulbs use so much less electricity than old incandescent bulbs for the same light?
choices: Incandescent bulbs waste most of their energy as heat; LEDs turn most of it into light
questions.explain: An incandescent filament glows because it is white-hot: about 90 percent of the energy becomes heat. An LED makes light directly in a semiconductor.
questions.tip: Old bulbs are tiny heaters that happen to glow.

questions.q: Why do most touchscreens not respond to a plastic pen or a gloved finger?
choices: They sense the electrical conductivity of your skin, which a plastic pen or ordinary glove lacks
questions.explain: Capacitive screens detect the small change in electric field when a conductor (your finger) touches the glass. Touchscreen gloves have conductive fingertips.
questions.tip: Touchscreens feel your electricity, not your push.

questions.q: How does a solar panel make electricity?
choices: Light knocks electrons loose in a silicon semiconductor, creating a current
Sunlight heats water that drives a generator
Mirrors focus light into a battery
The panel stores heat and releases it as power
questions.explain: This is the photovoltaic effect. Panels work on cloudy days too, just with less output.
questions.tip: Photo (light) plus voltaic (electricity): light in, current out.

questions.q: An electric motor and a generator are...
choices: The same idea in reverse: a motor turns current into motion, a generator turns motion into current
questions.explain: Both rely on the link between electric current and magnetic fields. Spin a motor by hand and it produces a voltage.
questions.tip: Motor: electricity in, spin out. Generator: spin in, electricity out.

questions.q: What are the white trails that airplanes sometimes leave across the sky?
choices: Condensation trails: water vapor from the engines freezing into ice crystals in the cold air
questions.explain: At cruising altitude the air is far below freezing. Whether a contrail forms and how long it lasts depends on the humidity up there.
questions.tip: Contrail = condensation trail, a man-made cirrus cloud.

questions.q: How does a nuclear power plant make electricity?
choices: Splitting uranium atoms releases heat that boils water into steam, which spins a turbine
The radiation is collected directly as electricity
Fusion of hydrogen heats the reactor
questions.explain: The nuclear part only makes heat. From the steam onward, it works like a coal plant: turbine, generator, power lines.
questions.tip: Nuclear plant: a very fancy kettle.

questions.q: Fiber-optic internet cables carry data as...
choices: Pulses of light inside thin glass fibers
questions.explain: The light bounces along inside the glass by total internal reflection, carrying far more data over longer distances than copper.
questions.tip: Fiber optics: the internet travels as flashes of light.

questions.q: Why does a humid day feel hotter than a dry day at the same temperature?
choices: Sweat evaporates more slowly in humid air, so it cools you less
Water vapor holds heat against your skin
Your body makes more heat in humidity
questions.explain: Evaporating sweat is your main cooling system. The heat index combines temperature and humidity to give the 'feels like' number.
questions.tip: Sweat only cools you if it can dry.

questions.q: What does wind chill describe?
choices: How much faster wind carries heat away from your skin, making it feel colder
A drop in the actual air temperature caused by wind
The temperature at which wind freezes
How cold the wind itself is
questions.explain: Wind strips away the thin layer of warm air next to your skin. A thermometer in the wind still reads the real air temperature.
questions.tip: Wind chill is about your skin, not the thermometer.

questions.q: Why is it colder on top of a mountain, even though it is closer to the Sun?
choices: Air pressure is lower, so rising air expands and cools, and the thin air holds less heat
It is farther from Earth's warm core
questions.explain: Temperature drops roughly 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometer of height. The extra closeness to the Sun is tiny compared with 150 million kilometers.
questions.tip: Up a kilometer, down about 6 degrees.

questions.q: A forecast says '30 percent chance of rain'. That means...
choices: There is a 30 percent chance that measurable rain will fall at any given spot in the forecast area
It will rain for 30 percent of the day
30 percent of the area will definitely get rain
questions.explain: The probability of precipitation is about whether it rains at your location in the period, not how long or how hard.
questions.tip: 30 percent: three days in ten like this one, you'd get wet.

questions.q: Hurricane categories (1 to 5) are based on...
questions.explain: The Saffir-Simpson scale starts at 74 miles per hour for Category 1 and reaches Category 5 at 157 mph. Flooding, not wind, often causes the most damage.
questions.tip: Category = wind. The number says nothing about the rain or the size.

questions.q: What is El Nino?
choices: A periodic warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean that shifts weather patterns around the world
A hurricane that forms in the Pacific
A cold current along South America
questions.explain: El Nino years tend to bring wetter winters to the southern United States and drought to parts of Australia and Indonesia. La Nina is the cool phase.
questions.tip: El Nino: warm Pacific water, weather goes sideways worldwide.

questions.q: What is the difference between a tornado watch and a tornado warning?
choices: A watch means conditions are favorable; a warning means one has been seen or detected on radar, so take shelter
A warning is less serious than a watch
A watch means a tornado has touched down
questions.explain: The same applies to severe thunderstorm and flood alerts: watch means be ready, warning means act now.
questions.tip: Watch: be alert. Warning: take cover now.

questions.q: The safest thing to do when you hear thunder is...
choices: Go indoors or into a hard-topped car, and stay there 30 minutes after the last thunder
Lie flat in an open field
Keep swimming, since water is safe
questions.explain: If you can hear thunder, lightning is close enough to strike. Trees, open fields and water are the worst places.
questions.tip: When thunder roars, go indoors.

questions.q: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. Why is it winter in the Northern Hemisphere then?
choices: Seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis, not its distance from the Sun
The Sun is cooler in January
The oceans absorb the extra heat
questions.explain: In January the Northern Hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, so sunlight hits it at a low angle for fewer hours. The 3 percent change in distance barely matters.
questions.tip: Tilt makes the seasons; distance is a red herring.

questions.q: The jet stream is...
choices: A band of fast, high-altitude winds that steers weather systems from west to east
A river of warm water in the Atlantic
The trail behind a jet plane
A wind that blows only in summer
questions.explain: Jet streams blow at over 160 kilometers per hour near the top of the troposphere. Flights from the United States to Europe ride them and are faster eastbound.
questions.tip: The jet stream is the weather's conveyor belt, west to east.

questions.q: The dew point is...
choices: The temperature at which the air would become saturated and dew or fog forms; higher means muggier
The point where rain turns to snow
The lowest temperature of the day
questions.explain: A dew point above about 18 degrees Celsius (65 Fahrenheit) feels sticky to most people. It is a better comfort guide than relative humidity.
questions.tip: High dew point, sticky day.

questions.q: Do humans use only 10 percent of their brains?
choices: No: brain scans show activity across virtually the whole brain over a day
questions.explain: Different regions handle different jobs, but nearly all of them are active. Damage to almost any area causes some loss of function.
questions.tip: You use all of your brain, just not all at once.

questions.q: Can lightning strike the same place twice?
choices: Yes: tall structures like the Empire State Building are hit many times a year
questions.explain: Lightning favors tall, pointed, conductive objects, so the same spots get hit again and again.
questions.tip: Lightning loves a repeat: tall and pointy gets hit again.

questions.q: Is the Great Wall of China visible to the naked eye from space?
choices: No: it is long but too narrow to see from orbit without magnification
Yes, it is the only man-made object visible
questions.explain: The wall is only a few meters wide and similar in color to the land. Astronauts report seeing cities and highways more easily.
questions.tip: Long is not the same as wide: the wall is a thread from orbit.

questions.q: Are bats blind?
choices: No: bats can see, and many also use echolocation to hunt in the dark
Yes, but they have excellent hearing to make up for it
questions.explain: Many bats see well, and fruit bats in particular rely on sight and smell. Echolocation adds to their vision rather than replacing it.
questions.tip: 'Blind as a bat' is an insult to bats.

questions.q: How long is a goldfish's memory?
choices: Months: goldfish can learn and remember feeding times and routes
questions.explain: In experiments goldfish learned to push a lever for food and remembered it weeks later.
questions.tip: Goldfish remember far longer than the three-second myth.

questions.q: Does cracking your knuckles cause arthritis?
choices: No: studies have found no link between knuckle cracking and arthritis
Yes, but only in the fingers you crack
Only if you start before age 10
questions.explain: The pop is a gas bubble forming in the joint fluid. One doctor cracked the knuckles of one hand for 60 years with no difference between hands.
questions.tip: The knuckle pop is just a bubble, not bone damage.

questions.q: Did humans and non-bird dinosaurs ever live at the same time?
choices: No: the last non-bird dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, long before humans
questions.explain: Modern humans appeared roughly 300,000 years ago. Birds are living dinosaurs, so in that sense chickens count.
questions.tip: Dinosaurs: 66 million years ago. Humans: 300 thousand. No overlap, except birds.

questions.q: Does sugar make children hyperactive?
choices: Controlled studies find no effect on behavior; the belief itself shapes what parents notice
questions.explain: In blind trials, children given sugar or a sugar-free substitute behaved the same, but parents who were told their child had sugar rated them as more hyperactive.
questions.tip: The sugar rush is in the parents' expectations, not the kids.

questions.q: Does water drain in the opposite direction in the Southern Hemisphere because of the Coriolis effect?
choices: No: the Coriolis effect is far too weak at sink size; the basin's shape and how the water was moving decide it
Yes, but only at the equator
questions.explain: Coriolis matters for hurricanes hundreds of kilometers wide. In a sink, tiny leftover swirls from filling it dominate.
questions.tip: Coriolis spins hurricanes, not your bathtub.

questions.q: Is the tongue divided into zones that each taste only one thing (sweet at the tip, bitter at the back)?
choices: No: all taste types can be detected across the whole tongue
Yes, exactly as the classic diagram shows
questions.explain: The 'tongue map' came from a mistranslation of a 1901 German paper. Sensitivity varies slightly, but every region tastes everything.
questions.tip: The tongue map is a myth: taste is everywhere on the tongue.

questions.q: Is glass a slow-flowing liquid, which is why old windows are thicker at the bottom?
choices: No: glass is an amorphous solid, and old panes are uneven because of how they were made
Yes, which is why old windows are blurry
questions.explain: Old window glass was spun or blown and cut unevenly; glaziers often put the thick edge at the bottom. Some old panes are thicker at the top.
questions.tip: Old windows are wobbly because of the glassmaker, not gravity.

questions.q: Could a penny dropped from the top of a skyscraper kill someone below?
choices: No: air resistance limits it to about 50 to 80 kilometers per hour, enough to sting but not injure
Yes, if dropped from above 100 floors
questions.explain: A penny is light and flat, so it reaches a low terminal velocity and tumbles. Heavier, denser objects are a different story.
questions.tip: A falling penny stings; it doesn't kill.

questions.q: What is CRISPR?
choices: A gene-editing tool that can cut DNA at a chosen spot so a gene can be removed, changed or added
questions.explain: CRISPR was adapted from a defense system bacteria use against viruses. The first CRISPR-based therapy, for sickle cell disease, was approved in 2023.
questions.tip: CRISPR: molecular scissors for DNA.

questions.q: How do mRNA vaccines work?
choices: They give cells temporary instructions to make a harmless piece of the virus, which trains the immune system
They inject a weakened live virus
They contain antibodies made in a lab
questions.explain: The mRNA never enters the cell nucleus and breaks down within days. Your cells make the protein, your immune system learns it, and the mRNA is gone.
questions.tip: mRNA vaccines: a recipe card the cell reads and then shreds.

questions.q: The James Webb Space Telescope mainly observes in...
questions.explain: Infrared passes through dust and reveals the most distant galaxies, whose light has been stretched to longer wavelengths by the expansion of the universe. The telescope must stay very cold to see it.
questions.tip: Webb sees in heat-light (infrared), so it hides in the shade and stays cold.

questions.q: An exoplanet is...
choices: A planet orbiting a star other than the Sun
A planet that has left its orbit
questions.explain: Thousands have been confirmed since the 1990s, many by watching a star dim slightly as a planet passes in front of it.
questions.tip: EXO means outside: planets outside our solar system.

questions.q: Why is antibiotic resistance growing?
choices: Bacteria evolve: those that survive antibiotic use multiply, and overuse speeds this up
Antibiotics get weaker as they age
questions.explain: Every course of antibiotics is a round of natural selection. Finishing prescriptions as directed and not using antibiotics for viral illnesses slows resistance.
questions.tip: Antibiotic resistance is evolution happening in real time.

questions.q: Why does carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels warm the planet?
choices: It is a greenhouse gas: it lets sunlight in but absorbs heat radiating back from the surface
It blocks sunlight from reaching the ground
questions.explain: This was measured in the laboratory in the 1850s and 1860s. Atmospheric CO2 has risen from about 280 parts per million before industry to over 420 today.
questions.tip: CO2 works like a blanket: thicker blanket, warmer planet.

questions.q: When a study is 'peer reviewed', that means...
choices: Other experts in the field examined it for errors before it was published
It was voted on by the public
questions.explain: Peer review catches many mistakes but is not a guarantee; findings gain trust when other groups replicate them.
questions.tip: Peer review: checked by rivals before it's printed.

questions.q: A headline says 'Coffee drinkers live longer'. What is the most careful reading?
choices: Coffee drinking is correlated with longer life; it may not be the cause
questions.explain: Observational studies cannot rule out that coffee drinkers differ in income, health or habits. Causation needs controlled experiments or very careful adjustment.
questions.tip: 'Linked to' in a headline means correlation, not cause.

questions.q: Gravitational waves, first detected in 2015, are...
choices: Ripples in space-time from events like two black holes merging
Waves on the surface of the Sun
questions.explain: Einstein predicted them in 1916. The LIGO detectors sensed a stretch of space smaller than a proton's width. The discovery won the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics.
questions.tip: Gravitational waves: space itself wobbling when black holes collide.

questions.q: The Higgs boson, discovered in 2012 at CERN, is linked to...
choices: How fundamental particles get their mass
questions.explain: Particles gain mass by interacting with the Higgs field. The Large Hadron Collider found the boson about 48 years after it was proposed.
questions.tip: The Higgs field is the molasses that gives particles mass.

questions.q: When a news story says a result is 'statistically significant', it means...
choices: The result is unlikely to be due to chance alone, not that it is necessarily large or important
Everyone in the study was affected
questions.explain: With a large enough sample, even a tiny, unimportant difference becomes statistically significant. Ask about the size of the effect too.
questions.tip: Significant means 'probably real', not 'probably matters'.

questions.q: Microplastics are...
choices: Plastic fragments smaller than 5 millimeters, found in oceans, soil and food
questions.explain: They come from larger plastics breaking down, from synthetic fabrics and from tire wear. Their health effects are still being studied.
questions.tip: Micro-plastics: plastic confetti, under 5 millimeters.
